reasons: New signal: exofop_tois, exofop_ctois and published_signal are all empty, and the verification record shows no TOI, CTOI, TCE or TESS EB match in the catalogues of 2026-10-15.

The dip is real in the data and recovered independently: other_sector_results S106 SPOC SNR 14.0 (expected 10.3) and S107 SPOC SNR 11.8 (expected 11.4); joint_search_snr 11.8 against joint_search_highest_null_snr 7.0; odd_even_difference_sigma 0.07; sector_depth_consistency_p_value 0.406; fit_depth_ppm 352 +/- 31.

Planet-sized and not grazing: planet_radius_earth_radii 3.91 +/- 0.23 (well below the 22.4 stellar limit), transit_grazing False, fit_impact_parameter 0.450, stellar_density_fit_to_tic_ratio 1.32 and fitted_to_expected_scaled_semi_major_axis 0.74 are both consistent with a transit of the target.

Ellipsoidal caution is physically inconsistent with a planet of this size: ellipsoidal_amplitude_ppm 126 +/- 31 (4 sigma; by sector S98 48 +/- 108, S106 129 +/- 43, S107 137 +/- 48) gives ellipsoidal_companion_mass_solar_masses 0.00332, about 3.5 Jupiter masses, which a 3.91 Earth-radius body cannot have. Either the term is stellar variability or the transiting body is not a planet. Gaia RV cannot separate these: gaia_rv_companion_mass_upper_limit_solar_masses 0.0707 is far above 0.0033, and gaia_rv_variable is False only because gaia_vbroad_km_s 270.8 makes the RVs imprecise.

The star is a very rapid rotator with strong pulsation: gaia_vbroad_km_s 270.8 with stellar_radius_solar_radii 1.93. The all-sector figure (tic121564843_0.81803.png) shows coherent oscillations of roughly 2000 ppm amplitude and about 1.2 h period in the phase-0.5 panel and in the binned points of all three sector panels, several times larger than the 352 ppm transit. That they fold coherently at 0.818 d across sectors months apart means the pulsation frequency is commensurate with the candidate period, so the dip and the P/2 ellipsoidal term could both be products of the stellar pulsation rather than of a companion. None of the ten automatic steps tests for this.

Pixel check: pixel_verdict unresolved, joint_difference_image_snr 5.4, joint_best_source Gaia DR3 2978034081419676416, per-sector SNRs 4.0 / 2.5 / 3.0 / 3.0 and an IndexError for S109. In the figures, S98 and S107 put the difference signal on the target pixel with the free-fit cross at the target, while S106 and S108 are dominated by gradients. I disagree with the weight the mechanical decision gives this caution: gaia_neighbours_able_to_cause_dip says the G 18.9 star at 39 arcsec needs an 88% eclipse, which is physically implausible, and nfpp_mean is 0. The images still cannot exclude an unresolved companion within the target's pixel, but the named neighbour is not the real concern.

TRICERATOPS fpp_mean 3.163e-09, most_likely_scenario TP on TIC 121564843, nearby_scenarios_excluded False: I give this little weight because TRICERATOPS assumes the dip is an astrophysical transit on the target or a catalogued neighbour; it does not model a pulsation-induced false alarm, which is the main open question here.

What would decide it: (a) prewhiten the pulsation modes in the S98, S106 and S107 light curves and re-run the search and fit; if 1/0.818 d is a difference or harmonic of the pulsation frequencies, or the dip does not survive with a flat out-of-transit baseline, drop; if a 352 ppm box transit survives, propose; (b) refit the P/2 term after prewhitening to see whether the 126 ppm ellipsoidal amplitude persists; (c) add S108 and S109 SPOC light curves to step 9 when released (sectors_used is 98 106 107 while the pixel check already reached 108 and 109; the S108 cutout depths of 11 +/- 158 and 7 +/- 163 ppm are consistent with zero but not yet conclusive) and fix the S109 pixel error to raise the difference-image SNR.
